<reason>Side B (CON) built and sustained the cleaner path to victory. The opening frame that the climate regime runs on consensus, not votes, was the decisive structural move, and B sharpened it each round: the diagnosis/prescription mismatch (a heavier placard doesn't staff parallel negotiating streams), the distinction between inclusive thresholds and zero-sum proportional shares, and especially the "pinch" (weight heavy enough to matter empties the room of emitters; light enough to keep them changes nothing). A's attempts to escape—shrinking the weighting, embracing an honest formula that includes Bangladesh and the Netherlands—were turned against A, with B forcing the dilemma between principled breadth and island privilege. B also answered A's pressure honestly: the capacity-funding remedy blunted the "status quo defense" charge, and the loss-and-damage fund directly answered the demand for a persuasion-delivered outcome. A's strongest moves (the Kyoto walkaway symmetry, "settled once," the concessions framing) were real but never neutralized the consent pinch, and A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for exceeding the word limit, an execution cost on top of an already-trailing position. A's closing was crisp, but B's closing crystallized the clash more decisively around compulsory consent versus unenforceable tallies. Neither side used fake citations; B's grounding was consistently plausible and proportionate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 ([B2.1]-[B2.3]): the observation that A's own portrait of consensus dysfunction describes informal power untouched by vote weight, plus the categorical distinction between inclusive thresholds and zero-sum proportional rankings, reframed the entire measurement dispute and set up the closing pinch A never escaped.</best_rebuttal>
